newsitem.title: USA: August, a month of political promises in Mass..
newsitem.headline: August, a month of political promises in Mass..

text.p: Paul Cellucci began his first full week as acting governor of Massachusetts on Monday and it is expected to be a busy one.
During his first three days as chief executive, Cellucci last week called for a huge cut in the state income tax.

With now citizen William Weld in Washington lobbying for a hearing to become the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Cellucci announced that the first bill he will file as chief executive calls for a cut in the state income tax to pre-1989 levels.
Over the next three years, the rate would gradually be dropped from 5.9 percent to 5 percent under the plan.

The rate had been 5 percent in 1989 when it was hiked to bail the state out of near bankruptcy. At the time, lawmakers said the increase was only temporary and the rate would fall back once deficit reduction bonds were retired. That will occur this fiscal year.
Worried that legislators would not keep their word and reduce the income tax, anti-tax groups are mounting a drive to place the tax cut on the 1998 statewide ballot.

That may account for last week's reaction to Cellucci's call by Democratic leaders of both the House and Senate. Both Speaker Thomas Finneran and Senate President Thomas Birmingham said they would be willing to consider the bill and might have some other tax-cutting ideas of their own.

When he unveiled his proposal, Cellucci said he hoped to persuade lawmakers that the $1.2 billion tax cut is warranted since revenue collections continue to exceed projections, creating huge budget surpluses.
In a gesture toward organized labor, Cellucci also indicated a possible softening of the administration's push to privatize more and more state services.
And he appeared favorably inclined to a suggestion from James Carlin, chairman of the Board of Higher Education, that a two-year community college education be offered tuition-free.
The acting governor will likely continue lobbing old and new initiatives into the public arena as he tries to become more visible to voters whose support he will seek next year.
The 1998 gubernatorial race promises to be a bruising one.

State Treasurer Joseph Malone, a fellow Republican, is already campaigning to dislodge Cellucci from the Corner Office, and Attorney General Scott Harshbarger plans to battle Congressman Joseph Kennedy on the Democratic side.
